w: What's tested Accepted schemes; copy the existing guidance when there are no signs or symptoms MIP facts (17.5 minutes a day, 1,800 chewing strokes, 500 swallowing contacts); PDL senses 20 µm What to check in working, non-working and protrusive movements Conformative vs reorganized: when to use each, CR vs MIP records, registration materials and errors Restoration by restoration: intracoronal, single crowns (bounded and end of arch), three-unit, quadrants, Class III and IV composites, anterior crowns, the custom anterior guide table Closest speaking space; natural tooth vs implant movement; anterior vs posterior implant occlusion "It really comes down to applying occlusion... where the rubber hits the road," mostly in restorative dentistry (based on Dr. Perng-Ru Liu's presentation). Patients rarely fit the textbook: tipped teeth give protrusive interferences, and problems such as wear facets, fractures through crowns and mobility often exist before symptoms do. Replacing a fractured crown doesn't fix the force that broke it. Schemes and guidance Accepted occlusal schemes: balanced (dentures; tried on teeth once, "bad idea"), mutually protected, and group function (today a canine, lateral and maybe the first premolar, not every tooth). Group function or canine guidance? In the absence of signs or symptoms, copy the existing guidance when restorations are needed. That is conformative dentistry. MIP is the complete intercuspation regardless of condylar position, the end of the chewing cycle, where maximum chewing force is applied and the mandible is stabilized to swallow, and it is not stable over the long term. In a day the teeth meet in MIP for only about 17.5 minutes: about 1,800 chewing strokes and 500 swallowing contacts (657,000 chewing strokes a year). Clenching is the pathologic exception. Healthy contacts mean no mobility, no wear, no fractures. In lateral excursions, check working contacts (canine guidance or group function) for mobility of the guiding teeth (splinting?) and for smooth vs restricted movement; contacts back in the posterior from plane problems, drifting or tooth loss hurt muscle function. A non-working contact tends to guide the mandible during lateral excursion; check mobility on the non-working side and the corresponding working contacts. A patient who has adapted to one over years can keep it, but patients don't tolerate one you introduce in an afternoon; reshape with enameloplasty when needed. The PDL detects material down to about 20 µm. In protrusion, check the direction, mobility, and any posterior contact: posterior protrusive interferences must be eliminated before restoring the anterior teeth. Sometimes anterior contours can give enough separation, but you can't make guidance steep enough to clear a badly tipped molar. Two approaches Idea Restoration in harmony with the existing jaw relationships The entire occlusal scheme is changed, in harmony with new jaw relationships Allowed changes Localized only: shorten an opposing cusp, eliminate non-working interferences, remove a deflective contact on the tooth to be restored Start "from ground zero" with the joints seated first: a reproducible starting point, an even stable occlusion, no iatrogenic deflective contacts Record MIP record: for working casts; as minimal as required CR record (bimanual manipulation): also for mounting diagnostic casts When Most general dentistry, if the occlusion is healthy and asymptomatic When conforming is unsafe: destruction, wear, fractures, or large multi-quadrant work How do you know conformative is safe? At diagnosis, compare the contact with the joints seated (CO) with the MIP contact; a big or deviating difference plus wear, fracture, mobility or tooth movement says copying is not enough. Registration materials: elastomeric PVS (Regisil), thermoplastic waxes (Aluwax), zinc oxide eugenol plaster, acrylics and plaster of Paris. PVS is an excellent impression material but sets in 20-30 seconds while the patient moves; warmed wax chilled with the air-water syringe hardens in 1-2 seconds. Common errors: a full-arch registration (you've put material between teeth that should touch) and untrimmed excess (you can't verify the mounting). A correct MIP record sits only where teeth are not in contact (the preps), is trimmed to the cusp tips and kept off soft tissue, and the contacts you see in the mouth (e.g. #26 on #8) must show on the mounting. With elastomers: constant occlusal pressure while setting, trim with a scalpel before mounting, and press the casts while mounting to avoid rebound. Best of all, hand-articulate when you can: "any material that we use is going to increase error." Posterior restorations For any posterior intracoronal restoration you want a stable relationship with the opposing tooth and simultaneous contacts with the other teeth in MIP. You don't want deflective contacts, high spots, infraocclusion (the tooth will supererupt, "and it never supererupts in a good contact"), non-working contacts or working interferences. Single intracoronal: small, fit the existing relationships. Large, check the opposing cusp for over-eruption and non-working contacts and make localized adjustments before placing it. Multiple intracoronal: conformative for multiple small restorations without an over-erupted cusp. Localized modification for an over-erupted cusp into a worn or scooped-out restoration, non-working contacts, plunger cusps (cusps violating the plane of occlusion) and deflective contacts. Reorganized for multiple large restorations in posterior quadrants (use materials with high initial compressive and tensile strength). Single bounded crown: usually conformative; check and adjust the opposing cusp first; registration by hand articulation, PVS or Aluwax; no face-bow; hinge-type articulator (semi-adjustable rarely). At try-in: fully seated, proximal contacts first, then occlusion. Single crown at the end of the arch: the same, except adjust any retruded deflective contact first and use an occlusal registration to mount (the cast easily drops posteriorly). Three-unit bridge (bounded or end of arch): usually conformative (generally fine up to three units in the posterior); ensure the opposing arch has a desirable occlusal plane; PVS or Aluwax; semi-adjustable (arcon) articulator, hinge sometimes OK. A four-unit bridge replaces about half the patient's occlusion, so "what do you put back?" Quadrants: ensure a desirable opposing plane (crown lengthening, opposing crowns, root canal therapy may be needed); more indication for equilibration first. Restoring opposing quadrants lets you build a favorable plane and curve of Spee. Articulators: "there's never an advantage to the dentist" of a small hinge articulator; the advantage is entirely the laboratory's. One the size of the patient, even a semi-adjustable left at average settings, makes arcs closer to the patient's, so less adjusting at the hardest place to work, beside the tongue. Anterior restorations Class III composite: copy the existing contacts; avoid centric and protrusive contact on the restorative material. Class IV composite: simultaneous centric and protrusive contact on the natural tooth AND the restoration to reduce fracture and differential wear, especially edge to edge. All the guidance on a Class IV is "a recipe for disaster." Single anterior crown: without symptoms, in harmony with the existing occlusion; correct posterior deflective contacts that slide the mandible forward into the incisors, especially with a history of fracture. Multiple maxillary anterior crowns: need a customized anterior guide table when restoring both central incisors or one or both canines. The guide pin's pathways capture the full functional range of the guidance. To copy the guidance unchanged, make the impression for the guide before preparing the teeth. Inadequate anterior guidance (missing, malaligned or broken-down anteriors): diagnostic wax-up at a tentative VDO → provisionals from its matrix (guidance and esthetics) → observe for several weeks (at least three if mild and asymptomatic; months for a bruxer) → custom anterior guide table from the corrected provisionals → definitive lingual contours follow the guide. The tentative VDO uses the closest speaking space: about 1-2 mm between the incisal edges while the patient unconsciously repeats "s" (counting 60 to 70). Too much space gives a lisp, too little a whistle. Implants An implant is a titanium root locked in bone, with no periodontal ligament, so it moves far less than a tooth: Apical About 28 µm About 2-3 µm (bone microstrain) Lateral 56-75 µm posterior; 90-108 µm anterior 10-50 µm Anterior implants: centric contact very light in casual intercuspation and equal to the neighbors in maximum intercuspation; in excursions avoid immediate canine disclusion and share the load with the natural teeth, which have proprioception. Posterior implants: very light in casual closure, equal in maximum intercuspation (no contact lets the opposing tooth supererupt); avoid contact in excursions if possible; mutually protected occlusion. Test with shimstock (about 12 µm): on a light closure it holds on the neighbors and pulls through the implant with some resistance; on a clench the teeth drop into their PDL and it holds on all of them. Summary: most of general dentistry is conformative, but look first. Check the opposing plane of occlusion, the contacts, any deflections and the direction of forces; copy what the patient has only if it is asymptomatic and healthy.
